newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Costello affirms Australian savings charge OK.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Costello affirms Australian savings charge OK.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello on Wednesday reaffirmed the government's belief that its new surcharge on the retirement savings of higher income earners was constitutional.
The only advice he had received was that it was constitutional, Costello said, a week after saying he would refer one lawyer's doubts to the government's advisers.
Leading lawyer Dennis Rose said last week the charge was unconstitutional because of the unusual manner in which it was imposed.

"The only legal advice I've received is that the bill, as drafted by the government, is within the constitutional power and the advice is that, even in the light of Mr Rose's opinions, that it's constitutional," Costello told parliament on Wednesday.
Costello said last week he would ask the government's lawyers to examine the points Rose had raised to see if they were valid.
But on the same day he also said the government's advisers had already considered and rejected the consititutional doubts Rose had expressed.

The surcharge on superannuation earnings was one of the many savings announced in Costello's August budget and was aimed at raising the concessional tax rate on superannuation contributions for people earning more than A$70,000 a year.
The current rate is only 15 percent -- well below the 48 percent top income tax rate -- and the government wants to raise it to 30 percent.
But the measure was imposed as a "surcharge" on superannuation funds, not as a tax on the income earner.

Rose, formerly the government's own chief lawyer, has said the measure therefore contravenes the constitution's requirement that the government take people's property on just terms, a provision that does not affect tax.
The legislation giving effect to the charge has not yet passed parliament and could still be easily amended.
It has applied since budget night, August 20, 1996 but the revenue would not flow to the government until the 1997/98 financial year.
